A review of whether NoteDown's end-to-end encryption holds what
`docs/sync-and-sharing.md` promises, done on 2026-10-30 before a release in
the Play Store. Findings H1–H4 were fixed the same day; the others are open,
each with what fixing it takes. The other docs describe the fixed state; this
file keeps the findings, their status and why.

## Scope and method

- **Read:** the client's cryptography and sync (`app/js/core/crypto.js`,
  `vault.js`, `sync-state.js`, `merge.js`, `app/js/sync/`), how untrusted
  content is rendered (`app/js/core/markdown.js`, the HTML sinks in
  `app/js/ui/`), the server (`server/notedown_server/`: `auth.py`, `app.py`,
  `protocol.py`, `admin.py`, `trmnl/`), the Android shell
  (`mobile/android/`: manifest, `VaultPlugin`, `PrivacyPlugin`,
  `ShareFilePlugin`, `QuickCapturePlugin`) and `.github/workflows/`.
- **Proven, not only read:** H1 and H2 against a local server with the
  app's own modules — a server named in an invitation link got a token for
  the victim's device on the real server, and an older ciphertext uploaded as
  a newer version was accepted and merged, dropping a note; H3 and H4 with
  the app's key-trust code (`openWrap`, `keyVerdict`) on real signed device
  lists and wraps. These scenarios are regression tests now (per finding).

## Threat model

End-to-end encryption has to hold against the server: its operator, someone
who took it over, a copy of its database (`docs/sync-and-sharing.md` →
"Principles"). Besides the server: someone who sends a link or shows a code,
a contact (a member of a shared file), someone holding a copy of a device
that signed out or was removed, and the network (TLS assumed). Out of scope:
a device compromised while in use, and the host that serves the web app's
code (a stated exception, "Principles").

## Findings

| # | Severity | Finding | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| H1 | High | The sign-in signature wasn't bound to the server: a token relayed through an invitation link | Fixed 2026-10-30 |
| H2 | High | A file's ciphertext wasn't bound to its file and version: the server could roll a file back | Fixed 2026-10-30 |
| H3 | High | A device list could be served cut back: a removed device was trusted again | Fixed 2026-10-30 |
| H4 | High | A signed-out device kept the power to hand out new file keys | Fixed 2026-10-30 |
| M1 | Medium | The safety code is a birthday target | Open |
| M2 | Medium | No Content-Security-Policy | Open |
| M3 | Medium | Prototype URL switches work in the deployed web app | Open |
| M4 | Medium | Inflating a file has no size limit (app and TRMNL plugin) | Open |
| M5 | Medium | The release signing key in every branch build; actions pinned by tag | Open |
| M6 | Medium | The relay message of linking a device isn't authenticated | Open |
| L1–L6 | Low | See "Low" | Open |

### H1 — a sign-in relayed through another server (fixed)

- **What:** a device signed `notedown-auth-v1:<challenge>` for whichever
  server it talked to, and an invitation link names the inviter's server
  (`srv=`). A link on the real web app's address with `srv` pointing
  elsewhere made the app sign in there once the user confirmed the contact
  request; that server passed on the real server's challenge and got a token
  for the victim's device, valid for an hour.
- **Impact:** no note text (the keys stay wrapped for devices), but the file
  list and the social graph (members, contacts, device lists), overwriting
  files and keys, H2's rollback, server-side contacts; with an admin's token
  the whole admin page (a restore that empties the server, news to everyone,
  blocking).
- **Fix:** the signature covers canonical JSON with the server's host, the
  identity and the device (`notedown-auth-v2`); the server checks it against
  the host of the request. Deleting with the recovery key likewise
  (`notedown-delete-v2`). `docs/server-api.md` → "Authentication"; apps
  before level 3 get 426 ("App versions").
- **Tests:** `server/tests/test_api.py` and `test_lifecycle.py` (a signature
  for another server, identity or device, or the old message, signs in and
  deletes nowhere), `tests/crypto.test.mjs`, `tests/api.test.mjs`.

### H2 — a file rolled back by the server (fixed)

- **What:** files were AES-GCM without associated data, and the client
  trusted the version the server reported. The server — or a relayed token
  (H1) with the version history's older states — could upload an older
  ciphertext as the newest version; every device decrypted it and merged it
  against its newer base, which dropped every note added since, silently
  and on all devices. `docs/sync-and-sharing.md` claimed the opposite.
- **Fix:** the associated data is the file ID and the version the upload
  creates, so a state opens only as that version. An older version served as
  itself counts as a restored server and is merged from scratch, which loses
  nothing. Files from before open only on a device that never saw a bound
  version of the file, or merges from scratch, and are uploaded again, bound.
  `docs/server-api.md` → "Keys".
- **Tests:** `tests/crypto.test.mjs` (another version or file doesn't open),
  `tests/sync-state.test.mjs` (`legacyFileAllowed`), `scripts/e2e-sync.js`
  ("an older state the server hands out as a newer version is refused").

### H3 — a device list served cut back (fixed)

- **What:** a client took any valid start of a device list and remembered
  nothing. Served without its removal, a removed (stolen) device was active
  again: its wraps were trusted, and the renewal after the removal wrapped
  the new key for it — likewise a contact's removed device when sharing.
- **Fix:** pins — per identity the length of the longest verified list and
  the hash of its last entry; a shorter list or another past is refused. An
  own append pins at once, so the renewal after a removal only takes a list
  with the removal on it. The own list is kept whole, and what a restored
  server lost is appended again. `app/js/sync/pins.js`, `docs/server-api.md`
  → "Device list".
- **Tests:** `tests/crypto.test.mjs` (`checkPin`).

### H4 — a signed-out device handing out keys (fixed)

- **What:** wraps signed by a device that signed itself out stayed trusted
  for any key generation, so a copy of it (the documented case: a public
  computer) together with the server or a relayed token could give every
  device a key of its own, and read every later change; a generation of
  2³²−1 also blocked every later renewal.
- **Fix:** a signed-out signer counts only for the key a device has already,
  or for a device without one (restoring after the last device signed out),
  which renews that key at once. `app/js/core/sync-state.js` → `keyVerdict`.
- **Tests:** `tests/sync-state.test.mjs`, `scripts/e2e-sync.js` ("Lea signs
  out … and are renewed at once").

### Medium (open)

- **M1 — safety code:** 20 digits from one hash over *both* identity IDs.
  Someone in the middle who knows both IDs beforehand needs two forged
  identities with equal codes — a collision: about 2·10¹⁰ PBKDF2 runs, some
  60 hours on one current GPU, not "too costly". Signal shows each identity's
  fingerprint on its own (2 × 30 digits), so a forger needs a second preimage.
  Fix: one half per identity.
- **M2 — no Content-Security-Policy:** the escaping of untrusted text (shared
  notes, news, names) is careful — the sinks that carry such data were
  checked — but it is the only layer between a note and every key. A meta CSP:
  `script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval'`, `connect-src` only the API (which
  would also have stopped H1), `object-src 'none'`, `base-uri 'none'`.
- **M3 — URL switches in production:** `?sample` replaces the stored notes and
  sync state (one link erases a browser's notes), `?api=` points the browser
  at another server for good; `?sync=off` and `?platform=android` too. Off in
  deployed builds.
- **M4 — inflating without a limit:** `DecompressionStream` in `crypto.js` and
  `zlib.decompress` in the TRMNL plugin inflate whatever a member uploaded: a
  2 MB file becomes about 2 GB, so a member can crash the others' apps, and,
  shared with a TRMNL display, the 512 MiB server instance. Cap the inflated
  size.
- **M5 — signing and CI:** pushes to `claude/**` build preview APKs with the
  release keystore, and third-party actions are pinned by tag. For the Play
  Store: Play App Signing (CI then holds only the upload key), the keystore
  secret in an environment limited to `main`, actions pinned by commit.
- **M6 — linking a device:** the relay message is sealed for the new device but
  signed by nobody. A malicious server with an identity of its own can, once
  the device was added to the real list, swap the message, so the new device
  joins that identity and its notes and later input go there. Fix: a secret in
  the QR code that the sealed message must hold.

### Low (open, or to disclose)

- **L1:** "notes are shared with contacts only" is enforced by the server
  alone; a malicious server can bring in a shared file of a non-contact with a
  name of its choosing. Members who aren't contacts show as strangers;
  consider marking such a file.
- **L2:** the TRMNL plugin decrypts on the server (`docs/sync-and-sharing.md` →
  "TRMNL"); in the Play Store's Data safety form those notes don't count as
  end-to-end encrypted.
- **L3:** copying the recovery key puts it on the clipboard: mark it sensitive
  (`ClipDescription.EXTRA_IS_SENSITIVE`).
- **L4:** news posts are plain text from the server, a phishing channel if the
  server is taken over.
- **L5:** dictation in the web app goes to the browser's speech service
  (Chrome: Google); the web app should say so.
- **L6:** `"restore": true` pins every state it replaces, and authenticated
  endpoints have no rate limit: an identity with version history can grow the
  database for 30 days.

## What holds

- AES-256-GCM with fresh random nonces; X25519 + ML-KEM-768 hybrid wrapping
  with one HKDF over both secrets and a hash of both ciphertexts and keys
  (libcrux-ml-kem); Ed25519 signatures over canonical JSON, pinned to the
  server by test vectors.
- The device list is a signed hash chain the server can't add a device to;
  wrapped keys are signed and bound to file, recipient and generation; contact
  requests can't be forged (the inviter's fingerprint is in the link, its
  secret never reaches the server); linking commits to the new device's ML-KEM
  key in the QR code.
- On Android: the vault's data key sealed by the Keystore (StrongBox where
  present), no system backup, screen security, incognito keyboard, dictation
  on the device and reminders without note text by default.
- Untrusted Markdown: raw HTML escaped, `javascript:` and `data:` links
  neutralised, media loaded only on a tap by default.

## The claim "at least as secure as Signal"

Files under long-lived keys can't reach it, so the store listing should word
it carefully. There is no forward secrecy: a recorded database plus a
recovery key or device found later opens every state of the version history
and after. The server knows the social graph (contacts, member sets), IP
addresses and times. Accurate: "notes are end-to-end encrypted; the server
stores only ciphertext", with the exceptions web app, TRMNL and metadata.

## Play Store

- Google Play's Data safety form needn't list data that leaves the device
  end-to-end encrypted, readable only by sender and recipient. Notes qualify;
  notes shared with TRMNL, IP addresses and identifiers don't.
- Signing as in M5 before the first upload.

## Not checked

- That `app/vendor/mlkem.wasm` and the other vendored bundles rebuild to the
  same bytes.
- Every HTML sink of the app (those carrying untrusted data were).
- The hosting settings (Google Cloud, Neon, GitHub repository rules) and a
  built APK.
